newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi urged to tackle red tape, speed reform.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi urged to tackle red tape, speed reform.

text.p: The World Bank and the United Nations, warning that developing economies do not have the luxury of time, urged Vietnam on Tuesday to press on with reform of its creaking public administration.
Delegates at a conference in Hanoi were told the communist government must cut red tape, snuff out corruption and improve the efficiency of its vast civil service down to the grassroots.

"It is clear that attention to public administration reform at the local level will be a very important part of the overall programme in the coming years if Vietnam is going to be successful in meeting its poverty alleviation goals," World Bank Resident Representative Bradley Babson said.
Vietnam embarked on reforms of its Soviet-style economy in 1986 by cautiously introducing market principles. It also opened doors which had long been closed to the outside world.
Those steps have brought huge rewards, with several years of vigorous economic growth, a flood of foreign investment and an increasingly sympathetic donor community.
But the government concedes that reform of public administration has not kept pace with the economic transition.

"Public administration reform continues to cope with inertia, obstacles created by customs, habits and old management methods of the centrally planned period," Minister Phan Ngoc Tuong said in a speech prepared for delivery at the conference.
Tuong heads the Government Committee on Organisation and Personnel and is also chairman of a four-year-old UN Development Programme steering committee on public administration reform.

Last year the government moved to streamline the multi-tiered administration, cutting the number of ministries to 22 from 27 and reducing the number of departments in provincial people's committees to 20 from more than 30.
It has also stepped up training in the civil service and last month approved a five-year masterplan for further training.
But bureaucracy, one of foreign investors' chief complaints, still acts as a huge brake on development.

"The existing public administration has been unable to make the necessary changes in time and has become a drag and a constraint on growth," Doan Trong Thuyen, vice-chairman of the UNDP project, said in a paper distributed at the conference.
Babson said that improving public sector management would only be possible if there were an all-out attack on corruption.
A report in March by the Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk Consultancy Ltd said that corruption in Asia was most common in Indonesia, China and Vietnam.
At its milestone congress four months ago, the Communist Party of Vietnam vowed to tackle both graft and bureaucracy. But specific measures were not spelt out in its congress manifesto.
The UNDP's resident representative in Hanoi, Roy Morey, told the conference that economies in transition could not afford to stand still while the world around them raced ahead.

"Vietnam needs the stability of a bicycle rider, not of someone standing fast in a fixed position," he said. "In regional terms, Vietnam's international position is not stable if it falls far behind its fast-growing neighbours."
